questions.stem: Which multiplication has the same answer as 10 + 10?
questions.stemText: Which multiplication has the same answer as 10 + 10 ?
questions.explain: Count the 10s: there are 2 of them, so this is 2 groups of 10, which is 2 × 10 = 20. Counting one group too many gives 3 × 10, which is 10 too much, and multiplying the wrong pair gives 10 × 10 or 3 × 2. Multiplication is a short way of writing the same number added over and over - that is the whole idea, and it is why the times tables are worth knowing by heart.

questions.stem: Xin Yi works out 4913 + 1771 in columns. One column makes 16, so she writes 6 in that column and a small 1 above the column on its left. How much is the 6 she writes there worth?
questions.stemText: Xin Yi works out 4913 + 1771 in columns. One column makes 16, so she writes 6 in that column and a small 1 above the column on its left. How much is the 6 she writes there worth?
questions.explain: The column that makes 16 is the hundreds column: 9 + 7 = 16, and no other column reaches ten. 16 hundreds is 1 thousand and 6 hundreds, so the 6 stays in the hundreds column - worth 600 - and the small 1 goes above the thousands column - worth 1000. The 6 is worth 600. A mark is worth the column it is written in, not the digit it looks like: that is what regrouping means, ten of something small becoming one of the next size up. Every wrong answer here is one of the two slips - the right digit read in the wrong column, or the wrong digit read in the right one.

questions.stem: Priya works out 44 + 42 in her head. She makes 50 first. 44 + 42 = 50 + ?
questions.stemText: Priya works out 44 + 42 in her head. She makes 50 first. 44 + 42 = 50 + ?
questions.explain: To get from 44 up to 50 you need 6, so 6 is moved across from the 42. That leaves 42 − 6 = 36, and 50 + 36 = 86. Whatever you give to one number you must take off the other, or the total changes. You could have rounded the 42 up to 50 instead and taken that amount off the 44: it is the same total either way, so it lands on the same answer.

questions.stem: Priya had some trading cards. She gave away 1623 of them, then bought 768 more. Now she has 3417. How many trading cards did she have at first?
questions.stemText: Priya had some trading cards. She gave away 1623 of them, then bought 768 more. Now she has 3417. How many trading cards did she have at first?
questions.explain: Start at the end and undo each step in reverse order. The last thing that happened was buying 768, so take those off: 3417 − 768 = 2649. Before that 1623 were given away, so put them back: 2649 + 1623 = 4272. Undoing means swapping the operation: + becomes −, and − becomes +.

questions.stem: A rectangular banner is 19 cm long and 8 cm wide. A notch 6 cm wide and 2 cm deep is cut out of the middle of one long side, so the notch does not reach either end. Along that side there is 4 cm of edge before the notch and 9 cm after it, and the banner is still 6 cm wide behind the notch. Every corner is a right angle. What is the perimeter of the banner now?
questions.stemText: A rectangular banner is 19 cm long and 8 cm wide. A notch 6 cm wide and 2 cm deep is cut out of the middle of one long side, so the notch does not reach either end. Along that side there is 4 cm of edge before the notch and 9 cm after it, and the banner is still 6 cm wide behind the notch. Every corner is a right angle. What is the perimeter of the banner now?
questions.explain: Walk the eight sides: 4 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 9 + 8 + 19 + 8 = 58 cm. Careful: this notch is in the middle of a side, not at a corner. The 6 cm taken out of the top edge is replaced by the 6 cm along the bottom of the notch, so that part of the walk is unchanged. But the two sides of the notch, 2 cm down and 2 cm back up, are brand new. Perimeter = 2 × (19 + 8) + 2 × 2 = 58 cm. A corner cut leaves the perimeter alone; a middle notch makes it longer.
